newsitem.title: Liberia: Liberia commission installed to run May 30 polls.
newsitem.headline: Liberia commission installed to run May 30 polls.

text.p: Liberia installed a seven-member independent commission on Wednesday to run elections next month after seven years of civil war in the West African nation, witnesses said.
The move ended weeks of bickering among Liberia's warring factions over leadership of the commission and marked a major step towards democracy in country ruled for years by the gun.

The Independent Elections Commission, sworn in by interim head of state Ruth Perry, is headed by Henry Andrews, a veteran Liberian journalist in his 50s. It includes three non-voting international members.

"The Independent Elections Commission is charged to ensure that elections are held on 30th May, 1997," declared Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, whose country leads the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG policing Liberia since 1990.
"We believe that this date is realisable and it is obtainable," Ikimi said at the ceremony held inside Monrovia's Executive Mansion presidential complex.

Two of Liberia's leading warlords blamed for the civil war which killed more than 150,000 people but who are now running for president -- Charles Taylor and George Boley -- attended. A third warlord and rival candidate, Alhaji Kromah, was absent.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said just over a week ago that prospects for peace in Liberia looked more promising than at any time since the outbreak of a multi-sided civil war in December 1989. He said efforts should now focus on elections.
The elections are a key element of a peace accord signed at Abuja, Nigeria, last August after more than a dozen previous agreements broke down.
Fighting has devastated Liberia's mining and rubber economy.

In a report to the Security Council, Annan recommended a three-month extension, until June 30, of the 92-member U.N. Observer Mission in Liberia which works with the 10,000-strong ECOMOG fielded by the Economic Community of West African States.
Three members of the elctions commission were appointed by the former warring factions and four from civil society.
The parliament to be elected will comprise a 64-member House of Assembly and a 26-member Senate. Voting will be on the basis of proportional representation.
